title: Three-tier kernel dispatch: tiny/medium/large row classification
description:
## Why
Profiling shows the short kernel (1 thread/row) takes 57-73% of formula_pow time at (4,4,6) and (4,8,3), despite handling only 3-21% of total terms. The bottleneck is serial per-row processing with no memory-level parallelism. Benchmarks confirm that simply changing groupsize (32 vs 256) doesn't help — the fix needs intra-row parallelism.

## What
Reclassify rows into three tiers and dispatch accordingly:
- tiny (<32 terms) → short kernel, 1 thread/row (existing)
- medium (32–255 terms) → long kernel with Val(32), 32 threads/row (warp-per-row)
- large (≥256 terms) → long kernel with Val(256), 256 threads/row (existing)

No new kernel code. The existing long kernel is already parameterized by Val{WS}.

## Files
- src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl (struct, cache, constructor, dispatch)
- test/FormulaPowTests.jl (verify medium_rows populated)
- benchmarks/formula_pow_vs_ntt_bench.jl (re-measure)

## Acceptance
- Existing tests pass.
- (4,4,6) and (4,8,3) show measurable improvement vs current.
- No regression on (4,4,2) and (5,5,2).
close_reason: Three-tier dispatch implemented in commit 519fa7e. FormulaPowPlan carries short_rows/medium_rows/long_rows with thresholds 32/256; formula_pow dispatches all three tiers. Benchmark showed 1.8-3x speedup on (4,4,6) and (4,8,3).

title: Run tests and benchmarks: n=4 d=4 pow=2,6
description: Run the test suite and benchmarks (oscar/CPU, GPU FFT, formula_pow) for n=4, d=4, pow=2 and pow=6. Report results.
notes:
Ran 2026-04-16 on RTX 3070 (post-three-tier commit 519fa7e). All FormulaPow tests pass (17/17: CSR-plan 3, CUDA correctness 7, hybrid CPU 7; Metal skipped — no device).

Benchmarks (median):
| case         | oscar CPU | formula_pow CUDA | NTT CUDA | row split (short/med/long) |
|--------------|-----------|------------------|----------|----------------------------|
| n=4 d=4 p=2  |  0.015 ms |        0.148 ms  | 1.017 ms | 165/0/0                    |
| n=4 d=4 p=6  |  1.627 ms |        1.161 ms  | 0.647 ms | 410/874/1641               |

Takeaways:
- (4,4,2): formula_pow 6.9x faster than NTT (all short rows; NTT fixed setup dominates), but oscar CPU still wins at this tiny size.
- (4,4,6): NTT 1.8x faster than formula_pow despite the three-tier dispatch speedup. formula_pow beats oscar CPU by 1.4x.
close_reason: Tests and benchmarks run — see notes for results table. 17/17 FormulaPow tests pass on CUDA. formula_pow dominates NTT at (4,4,2) by 6.9x; NTT wins at (4,4,6) by 1.8x.

title: Batching cutover and benchmark validation
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.5 (dispatcher).

== Scope ==

Add a batched benchmark and validate the design's expected wins.

== Tasks ==

1. Add a batched benchmark file (benchmarks/formula_pow_batch_bench.jl) that runs each of the four configs at B=1 and B=1000.
2. Measure end-to-end and per-kernel times. Confirm:
   - B=1 path matches current single-op performance (no regression).
   - B=1000 amortizes overhead correctly: measured per-call cost (total time / batch_size) should be much smaller than the single-op cost. The Julia/KA bookkeeping (~45 µs single-op) should drop below 1 µs per element when amortized over 1000.
   - K1 in batched short/medium tier hits >99% warp efficiency (verify via kernel time vs theoretical work bound).
3. Update ideas.md: mark #4 (short-row warp divergence) as landed via sort + K1.
4. Update ideas.md: mark #8 (kernel fusion / batching) as landed.

title: Dispatcher and batched formula_pow API entry point
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.3 (plan struct) and GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.4 (K1 kernel).

== Scope ==

Add the public API for batched invocation and the dispatcher logic that picks K1 vs K2 based on plan.batch_size.

API:
  formula_pow!(output, originals, plan, backend)        # mutating, batched
  formula_pow(originals, plan, backend)                 # allocating, returns output

For B=1, originals is a 1D vector and output is a 1D vector (or batch_size=1 stacked, document the convention).
For B>=1, originals is 2D (n_input, batch_size), output is 2D (num_out, batch_size).

Dispatch logic at plan build time (NOT per-call):
  - if batch_size == 1:
      use K2 for short+medium rows, K3 for long
  - if batch_size >= K1_THRESHOLD (~1000 by default; document the constant):
      use K1 for short+medium rows, K3 for long

The threshold is a hand-tuned heuristic. Add a kwarg on formula_pow_plan to override it for benchmarking.

== Done when ==

- Both formula_pow and formula_pow! work for B=1 (matches existing behavior) and B>=1000 (uses K1).
- Tests in GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.1 pass.
- The B=1 path through the new API is no slower than the current single-op formula_pow (no regression).
- Behavior at intermediate batch sizes (B=2 to B=999) is documented (probably routes to K2 since K1 isn't saturated yet) — not optimized, but correct.

title: K1 kernel: 1 thread/row, no reduction (batched-only)
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.1 (tests), GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.2 (sort), GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.3 (plan struct), and the padded CSR epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0.

== Scope ==

New kernel: 1 thread per (row × batch element). No reduction. Each thread:
1. Identifies its assigned (row, batch_element) from @index(Global, Linear).
2. Reads its row's data via the padded CSR (zd0 layout): row_max_fc, row_factor_offset, term_ptr.
3. Loops over the row's terms, accumulating into a register.
4. Writes the result to output[row, batch_element].

ndrange = num_tier_rows * batch_size. Tier rows already sorted by length (GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.2), so threads within a warp do similar work counts (>99% efficiency at B>=100, ~100% at B>=1000).

Inner loop benefits from padded layout: row_max_fc is small and constant per row, so the factor loop can be Val-specialized at a later optimization pass.

== Implementation sketch ==

@kernel function formula_pow_K1!(output, originals, plan_arrays..., tier_rows, batch_size)
    i = @index(Global, Linear)
    batch_idx = (i - 1) ÷ length(tier_rows) + 1
    tier_idx  = (i - 1) % length(tier_rows) + 1
    row = tier_rows[tier_idx]
    original = view(originals, :, batch_idx)
    # ... inner loop using padded CSR ...
    output[row, batch_idx] = result
end

(Exact ndrange axis assignment to be decided alongside memory layout in GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.3.)

== Done when ==

- Kernel compiles on CPU and CUDA backends.
- Passes the tests in GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.1.
- Achieves the warp-divergence-free behavior measured in the planning analysis.

title: Batched plan struct and memory layout for formula_pow
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.1 (tests) and the padded CSR epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0 (layout settled).

== Scope ==

Extend FormulaPowPlan to support batched invocation. batch_size becomes a plan-time parameter (static for the plan's lifetime).

  formula_pow_plan(n_vars, d, pow, backend; batch_size=1) -> FormulaPowPlan

New fields on the plan struct:
- batch_size::Int
- (any kernel-dispatch decision baked at plan time; e.g. which short/medium tier kernel: K1 or K2)

== Memory layout ==

Decide and document the input/output layout. Current candidate (subject to refinement during implementation):
- Input: stacked 2D buffer of size (n_input, batch_size). Coalesced reads across the batch dimension when warps stride across batch elements.
- Output: stacked 2D buffer of size (num_out, batch_size).
- 'original' varies across the batch; the plan (CSR) is shared.

The caller is responsible for arranging data in the documented layout. Document explicitly in formula_pow_plan docstring.

== Done when ==

- Plan struct accepts batch_size.
- Input/output buffer shape documented and validated at API entry (assert n_input dim, batch_size dim match).
- Plan struct still works for batch_size=1 (single-op users see no behavior change other than the new kwarg).

title: Sort short/medium tier rows by length at plan-build time
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.

Add a sortperm by row length to short_rows and medium_rows at plan construction. Output indexing is unchanged (rows are still keyed on the original output position via term_ptr); only the row-list arrays in the plan are reordered.

== Why ==

K1 (1 thread/row, batched-only) places adjacent rows of the row-list array in adjacent threads of a warp. Without sort, length spread within a warp is wide → 40-60% efficiency loss to divergence. With sort, lengths in a warp are nearly uniform → >99% warp efficiency at B>=100, perfectly saturated at B>=1000. See data on GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj.

For K2 (1 warp/row), each warp processes one row, so within-warp divergence does not apply. Sort is a no-op for K2's correctness or performance — but it is harmless. Sort the same way for both tiers; the K1 path benefits and the K2 path is indifferent.

== Implementation ==

In formula_pow_plan, after computing short_rows and medium_rows, do:
    short_rows  = short_rows[sortperm(row_lengths[short_rows])]
    medium_rows = medium_rows[sortperm(row_lengths[medium_rows])]

long_rows can be sorted too — for K3 the spread-by-length question is more about scheduler load balance than warp efficiency. Sort doesn't hurt; if anything, it provides predictable launch ordering for benchmarking.

== Done when ==

- Plan builder produces sorted tier arrays.
- Existing tests still pass (output unchanged).
- A test verifies the sort property (consecutive entries in short_rows are in non-decreasing length order).

title: Update formula_pow kernels to read padded-CSR layout
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-rvs (tests) and the padded-CSR plan builder bead.

== Scope ==

Rewrite formula_pow_short_kernel! and formula_pow_long_kernel! to read from the new padded layout. Drop monomial_ptr lookups.

== New inner loop (per term j the thread handles) ==

  base = row_factor_offset[row]
  N    = row_num_terms[row]
  fc   = row_max_fc[row]
  contrib = term_coeffs[j]
  j_local = j - term_ptr[row]   # 0-based within-row term index
  for kk in 0:fc-1
      idx = padded_indices[base + kk * N + j_local]
      deg = padded_degrees[base + kk * N + j_local]
      contrib *= original[idx] ^ deg
  end
  partial += contrib

The factor-index access is stride-1 across consecutive threads (since j varies stride-1 across the warp), giving coalesced 128-byte transactions. The fc trip count is data-dependent per row but bounded by pow; for small pow the compiler may unroll.

== Considerations ==

- row_num_terms can be derived from term_ptr (term_ptr[row+1] - term_ptr[row]); no new array needed if we compute on the fly.
- For the short kernel (1 thread/row, will be deprecated by GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b but still relevant if it lands first), the same inner loop applies; coalescing is moot at 1 thread but the unrolled trip count and lack of monomial_ptr reads still help.
- For the long kernel, the strided iteration (thread t starts at term_ptr[row] + t and steps by WS) means t directly gives j_local, which simplifies indexing.
- Power operation: leave Base.^ alone for now. ideas.md #5 (unrolled small-degree power) is a separate optimization that composes naturally with this layout but is out of scope here.

== Done when ==

- Both kernels build green and pass the GPUPolynomials.jl-rvs test suite end-to-end on CPU and CUDA backends.
- monomial_ptr is gone from the kernel signatures.
- A correctness diff against pre-change main is zero across all four benchmark configs.

title: Build padded-CSR plan builder for formula_pow
description:
Part of epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0. Blocked by GPUPolynomials.jl-rvs (correctness tests must land first).

== Scope ==

Add a new plan-construction path that produces the padded Level-2 layout. The Oscar expansion in generic_power_formula stays unchanged; only the post-processing of the expanded polynomial changes.

== Output arrays ==

Replace the current ragged Level-2 triple (monomial_ptr, monomial_indices, monomial_degrees) with:

  - row_max_fc::Vector{Int32}        # length = num_output_rows; row's max factor count
  - row_factor_offset::Vector{Int32} # length = num_output_rows + 1; base into the padded factor arrays
  - padded_indices::Vector{Int32}    # factor-major-within-row, padded with 1
  - padded_degrees::Vector{Int32}    # factor-major-within-row, padded with 0

Within each row's slab, the layout is column-major in factor index:
  padded_indices[row_factor_offset[i] + kk * row_num_terms[i] + j_local]
where j_local is the term index within the row (0-based) and kk is the factor index (0-based).

term_ptr and term_coeffs stay as they are (Level 1 is unchanged).

== Sentinel choice ==

Padding cells: idx=1, deg=0. Reads original[1] (always a valid 1-based index since plans only exist when n_input >= 1) and computes original[1]^0 = 1, neutral in the term product. Document this invariant in code.

== Plan struct ==

FormulaPowPlan grows the four new arrays and drops monomial_ptr/monomial_indices/monomial_degrees. Tier arrays (short_rows, medium_rows, long_rows) and workgroup_size knobs are unchanged.

== Cache compatibility ==

The module-level _formula_pow_cache changes shape (different tuple of arrays). Bump any format version constant if one exists; otherwise the in-session cache will rebuild on first call after the change, which is fine.

== Done when ==

- formula_pow_plan returns the new padded layout for all backends supported by Adapt.adapt.
- A unit test verifies that for a known small config (e.g. (3,2,3)), the padded arrays decode back to the same factor data as the ragged arrays.
- The padded plan can be passed to a placeholder kernel that just sums original[idx]^deg over all (idx, deg) cells and gets the same total as the ragged version (proves padding is neutral).

title: Comprehensive correctness tests for formula_pow (gates padded-CSR work)
description:
MUST LAND FIRST. Gates all implementation work in epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0.

Build out test/FormulaPowTests.jl into a comprehensive correctness suite that exercises the cases where a layout change is most likely to introduce bugs. The same suite must pass against both the current ragged CSR and the future padded CSR — this is what makes the swap safe.

== Required coverage ==

Configurations (all four benchmark cases plus targeted edge cases):
- (4,4,2): all-short tier, max fc = 2, mostly uniform per-row
- (5,5,2): all-short tier, max fc = 2, mostly uniform
- (4,8,3): three-tier mix, max fc = 3
- (4,4,6): three-tier mix, max fc = 6, ragged within rows
- Add at least one minimal config (e.g. (2,2,2) or (3,2,3)) so a failure prints small diagnostic data instead of a 12k-term row

Edge cases to deliberately hit:
- Rows with a single 1-factor term (no padding need)
- Rows with all max-fc terms (no padding waste)
- Rows mixing 1-factor and max-fc terms (padding actually exercised — the failure mode for a wrong padding sentinel)
- The single 'fully homogeneous' term (e.g. x_i^d for some i): a 1-factor term with deg = pow*d
- Output rows with exactly 32, 256, 512 terms (tier boundary edges)
- pow=1 (degenerate: output should equal input)

Validation:
- Compare GPU output against an Oscar.jl computation (poly = build_homog_poly(coeffs, n_vars, d); expected = poly^pow; compare coefficients in with_replacement_combinations order). The benchmark file already shows how to build the Oscar polynomial — extract that helper into the test file.
- Test on at least one CUDA device (CI-skip if unavailable). KernelAbstractions CPU backend should also pass — easy second target.

== Non-goals ==

- Performance assertions. This bead is correctness-only; benchmarking is in the cutover bead.
- Testing NTT path. Out of scope.

== Done when ==

- Tests run green against the current ragged CSR on both CPU backend and CUDA backend.
- Tests cover all configs and edge cases listed above.
- A targeted test exists for the padding-sentinel case (rows with mixed factor counts) that would catch a wrong neutral-element choice (e.g. failing to use deg=0 padding).
- runtests.jl picks up the new tests.

title: Padded Level-2 CSR layout for formula_pow (ideas.md #9)
description:
Move from ragged Level-2 CSR (monomial_ptr + monomial_indices + monomial_degrees) to per-row padded factor-major layout. This is a structural change that affects every formula_pow kernel.

== Layout target ==

For each output row, the row's terms get a 2D slab of shape [row_num_terms, row_max_fc] stored factor-major (column-major in factor index). Padding cells use idx=1, deg=0 so original[1]^0 = 1 is a neutral product element. The row_max_fc value lives in a per-row Int32 array.

Drops monomial_ptr entirely. Replaces the (monomial_indices, monomial_degrees) ragged pair with two padded arrays in factor-major-within-row layout, plus a per-row 'row_factor_offset' Int32 array giving each row's slab base.

== Why ==

1. Kernel inner loop becomes coalesced: stride-1 reads across the warp at each factor index. (Today's ragged layout has stride-row reads with data-dependent loop bounds.)
2. Inner factor loop has compile-time-known trip count (row_max_fc, can be passed as Val for short configurations), enabling unrolling.
3. monomial_ptr reads (2 per term) disappear.
4. Memory cost is small: per-row padding blowup is 0.8-14% in long tiers, 0.8-37% in short/medium tiers. Detailed table in ideas.md.

== Why per-row max (not tier-max, not pow2) ==

Coalescing depends on within-row layout (factor-major), NOT on row_max_fc divisibility. Per-row max minimizes blowup (especially in (4,4,6) long tier) without sacrificing coalescing. Pow2 padding wastes ~2x more memory for no actual alignment benefit (warp lane stride is 1 with factor-major; max_fc affects iteration stride which doesn't impact coalescing). Per-tier max is a slightly simpler kernel but costs a few percent more memory.

== Children (test-first) ==

1. Comprehensive correctness tests (must land first, gates everything else)
2. Padded-CSR plan builder
3. Update formula_pow kernels to read padded layout
4. Cutover and benchmark validation

Depends on every child; closes when all are done.

== Coordination ==

- Lands BEFORE GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g (tier redesign) so the tier rewrite is written against the new layout.
- Unblocks GPUPolynomials.jl-p1q (on-disk plan cache) once the layout is settled.
- Orthogonal to GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b (warp-per-row default for short tier) — that can land before or after.
- ideas.md #9 should be marked landed when this epic closes.

title: Implement warp-per-row as default for short tier in single-op formula_pow
description:
Concrete implementation: route the short tier (rows <32 terms) through the existing formula_pow_long_kernel! at WS=32 instead of the dedicated 1-thread/row formula_pow_short_kernel!.

Rationale (from profiling on RTX 3070):
- (4,4,2) — all-short workload, 165 rows, mean 3.82 terms: short kernel 69 µs → warp-per-row 25 µs (2.7x).
- (4,8,3) — short kernel was 47 µs / 35%% of kernel time; warp-per-row would drop to ~20 µs.
- (4,4,6) — short kernel 121 µs / 10%% of kernel time; warp-per-row would drop to ~50 µs.

The short kernel is latency-bound: 165-566 threads is 0.2-0.8%% of RTX 3070 in-flight capacity, ~1 warp per active SM, no warps to hide memory stalls. Warp-per-row gives 32x more threads in flight, which (despite ~88%% of compute being wasted on small rows) wins decisively because we're nowhere near compute-bound at this scale.

This is correct for the SINGLE-OP API. A separate, more compute-efficient strategy (8x4 subwarp, or 1x1 with many batched rows) is appropriate ONLY in a batched context — see GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj (batching). Both paths can coexist: warp-per-row for the single-op default, specialized kernels for the batched path.

Implementation:
- formula_pow currently calls formula_pow_short_kernel! when short_rows is nonempty (lines 338-345 of src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl). Change to dispatch via formula_pow_long_kernel! at WS=32, same way medium tier does (lines 347-354).
- Either remove formula_pow_short_kernel! entirely (cleaner), or leave it dead-coded for future batched-path reuse.
- Plan partition can collapse short and medium into one tier at WS=32 (rows <256), simplifying FormulaPowPlan.
- Test: existing test/FormulaPowTests.jl should pass unchanged.

Scope: single API change, preserves correctness, ~4 line diff to formula_pow + plan partition logic. Does NOT depend on the broader tier-redesign work in GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g — this is just collapsing short into medium. d3g separately covers adaptive WS_L for the long tier and other partition tuning.

Estimated end-to-end win:
- (4,4,2): ~27%% (44 µs saved)
- (4,8,3): ~11%% (27 µs saved)
- (4,4,6): ~7%% (71 µs saved)
close_reason: Routed short_rows through long_kernel at WS=32; removed dedicated short kernel. All FormulaPow CPU tests pass.

title: Batching support for formula_pow (K1 kernel + batched API)
description:
Reframed from ideas.md #8 (kernel fusion). The real lever is batched invocation: amortize per-call overhead AND unlock more efficient short-row strategies that don't make sense in the single-op API.

== Why batching is the right E ==

Per-call overhead breakdown (from CUDA.@profile on (4,4,2), 100 calls; see GPUPolynomials.jl-kf1):
- Short kernel (device):                       69 µs (43%% of 161 µs e2e)
- gpu_fill_kernel zero-init (device + launch): 14 µs (9%%)
- cuMemAllocFromPoolAsync:                      8 µs (5%%)
- cuLaunchKernel x N (host):                   15 µs (9%%)
- cuStreamSynchronize (host):                  17 µs (11%%)
- Julia/KernelAbstractions bookkeeping:       ~45 µs (28%%)  <- LARGEST overhead chunk

The Julia/KA layer (Adapt.adapt, NDRange construction, KA iterator setup, type checks) is 28%% of e2e on (4,4,2). It is paid once per formula_pow call regardless of work size. Batching folds N invocations of formula_pow into one call → bookkeeping paid once for N inputs.

Sync overhead (~17 µs) is also per-call. Batched: one sync at the end of all work.

== Dual-kernel design unlocked by batching ==

In single-op mode, warp-per-row (GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b) is the right short-tier default — it wins because we are LATENCY-BOUND, not compute-bound. With only 165-566 rows, we cannot afford to give each row only 4 threads; we need 32 to get warps in flight to hide memory stalls. Compute waste (~88%%) is irrelevant when we are 6000x off the compute roofline anyway.

Once batching aggregates many calls' rows, the row count multiplies (e.g. 100 batched (4,4,2) calls → 16,500 short rows). At that scale we have enough warps regardless, so we can finally afford to be compute-efficient:

- 1x1 kernel (1 thread/row) — efficient when we have >>10K rows; full compute utilization, full GPU occupancy via volume.
- 8x4 subwarp kernel (8 rows per warp, 4 threads/row) — fits the 2-4 term row distribution naturally. ~95%% compute efficiency vs warp-per-row's ~12%%.
- Warp-per-row stays useful for moderate-batch + few-tiny-row cases.

So the batched API likely wants 2-3 kernels with a partitioning step (similar to current tier system but tuned for batched volume).

== Open design questions ==

- API shape:
  - formula_pow_batch(originals::AbstractVector{<:CuVector}, plan, backend) -> Vector{CuVector}
  - formula_pow!(out_buf, in_buf, plan, backend) for streaming reuse
  - Both? Pick one first?
- Memory: how to lay out N inputs and N outputs on the GPU. Concatenated CSR-of-CSR? Stride? AoS vs SoA?
- Plan reuse: a single FormulaPowPlan applies to many inputs. Cache work between calls (kernel object, output shape).
- Tier dispatch in batched kernel: launch per-tier (like today) but with N x rows_per_tier ndrange? Or a fused dispatch-on-tier-id super-kernel? Profile both.
- Streams: should batching use multiple CUDA streams to overlap or stay single-stream?
- Interaction with GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g (tier redesign): batched path will likely want different tier boundaries than single-op (because available parallelism is much higher).
- Interaction with GPUPolynomials.jl-jhq (subwarp investigation): jhq becomes more interesting in this context. Might fold into this bead's scope.

== Dependencies / sequencing ==

- Depends on GPUPolynomials.jl-63i (output prealloc) — batching needs caller-provided buffers.
- Depends on GPUPolynomials.jl-kwd (skip zero-init) — fewer launches per batched call.
- Sequence after GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b (warp-per-row default) — that establishes the single-op baseline.
- Subsumes most of GPUPolynomials.jl-jhq (subwarp investigation) once a real implementation context exists.

Decide API shape FIRST — the kernel design follows the API shape, not the other way around.
notes:
Post-discussion refinements (2026-04-25):

- Batch size is static for intended use cases (large-scale computation). Plan construction takes batch_size as a parameter; the planner runs once at plan-time with both the (n,d,pow) static info AND the batch_size known. No per-call re-partitioning needed.

- Prealloc-for-batching is a separate responsibility from GPUPolynomials.jl-63i (which covers only the single-op output buffer). The batched API needs its own pre-alloc shape: either a stacked 2D buffer of size (batch_size, num_out), or a Vector of num_out-sized buffers. Decide the layout when picking the API shape — include this in this bead's scope.

- Unified plan type across single-op and batched: FormulaPowPlan grows a batch_size field; single-op is batch_size=1. Same plan type, same formula_pow! entry point.

- Kernel library starting set: K1 (1 thread/row, batched-only), K2 (warp-per-row WS=32 with shuffle reduce), K3 (block-per-row with adaptive WS_L ∈ {256, 512}). Add K4 (8×4 packing) only if K1 shows unacceptable compute waste in measurement. Reject 16×2 / 4×8 until evidence demands them.
Tier/kernel design locked in (2026-04-25):

== Use cases ==

Two regimes only: B=1 (single-op) and B>=~1000 (large-scale batch). No support targeted for intermediate batch sizes (the analysis showed nothing distinct happens there worth a special kernel).

== Kernel set ==

3 kernels total:
- K1: 1 thread/row, no reduction, batched-only. New kernel, small. Sort short+medium rows by length at plan time so within-warp divergence is negligible.
- K2: 1 warp/row at WS=32 with shuffle reduction. = current formula_pow_long_kernel! at WS=32.
- K3: 1 block/row, WS in {256, 512} adaptive. = current formula_pow_long_kernel! at WS=Val. WS pick handled in GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g.

NO packings (8x4 / 16x2 / 4x8). Sort + K1 hits >99% warp efficiency across all four benchmark cases at B>=100, perfectly saturated by B>=1000 (data: K1 warp-divergence analysis 2026-04-25). Packings only buy 5-15% in the intermediate regime that we don't target. See GPUPolynomials.jl-jhq closed with this rationale.

== Dispatch ==

- B=1: K2 for short + medium, K3 for long. K1 unused.
- B>=1000: K1 for short + medium, K3 for long. K2 unused.

K3 always handles long because per-thread serial work in a long row is too large to hide latency with K1 alone, regardless of batch size.

== Sort ==

Sort short_rows (and medium_rows for batched mode) by ascending row length at plan-build time. Cost: one sortperm per tier, free in absolute terms. This is the heterogeneity fix that supersedes ideas.md #4 originally, and it works correctly with K1 in the batched regime.

== Implementation ==

Most of the kernel work already exists or is filed:
- K2 = current long_kernel at WS=32. Just route short rows through it for B=1 (= GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b).
- K3 = current long_kernel at WS in {256,512}. Adaptive WS in GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g.
- K1 = new kernel, ~30 lines. Does not exist yet. Add as part of this bead's scope.
- Sort = one sortperm call in plan builder.
- Batching API + memory layout = the original scope of this bead.

Padded CSR (epic GPUPolynomials.jl-zd0) is a prerequisite — K1 in particular benefits heavily from compile-time-known inner trip count via the new layout.

Probable later optimization (out of scope for this bead): bucket-by-length-range for K1 with Val{N} specialization on the inner loop trip count. Enables loop unrolling, ~5-15%. Independent of the divergence fix that sort already provides.

title: Skip output zero-init in formula_pow
description:
formula_pow uses KernelAbstractions.zeros for the output, which dispatches gpu_fill_kernel (~12 µs/call on (4,8,3)).

The zero-init is redundant: short_rows ∪ medium_rows ∪ long_rows covers every output row (the CSR is built for all of with_replacement_combinations(1:n_vars, d*pow)), so every position gets written by exactly one kernel launch.

Change: swap KernelAbstractions.zeros for an uninitialized allocation (e.g. KernelAbstractions.allocate, or similar). Add a test that verifies every output index is touched by exactly one tier, to guard the invariant.

Estimated win: ~12 µs/call (~5%% on (4,8,3), ~1%% on (4,4,6)). Trivial change. Free win if the invariant check passes.
close_reason: Switched to KernelAbstractions.allocate (uninitialized) for output. Added partition invariant test that verifies short∪medium∪long covers 1:num_rows disjointly; if it ever breaks, uninit becomes unsafe and tests catch it.

title: Pre-allocate output buffer for formula_pow
description:
formula_pow currently calls KernelAbstractions.zeros(backend, eltype(original), num_out) on every invocation (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl line 333), going through cuMemAllocFromPoolAsync. Profile on (4,8,3) showed this takes 13-137 µs per call with high variance, contributing to p90=11x-median tail latency.

Change: accept an optional pre-allocated output buffer, or cache one on the FormulaPowPlan (with !-mutating formula_pow! variant that writes into a caller-provided buffer).

Estimated win: ~13-30 µs median saved (5-10%% on (4,8,3)), plus meaningful p90 reduction by eliminating one source of allocator-driven jitter.

Minimal API change. Pairs naturally with the zero-init removal (separate bead).
close_reason: Added formula_pow!(output, original, plan, backend) mutating variant that writes into a caller-provided buffer. formula_pow now allocates and delegates. Test seeds buffer with sentinel garbage and confirms every index is overwritten.

title: Profile formula_pow for (n_vars=5, d=5, pow=2)
description: Profile the (5,5,2) benchmark case on RTX 3070. Input has 126 monomials (vs 35 for (4,4,*)). Check whether the larger original array changes the bottleneck profile — is indirect-read pressure on original higher? Does the shmem-cache idea (idea #1 in ideas.md, previously a no-op on (4,4,6)) become worthwhile here?
notes:
Profile (5,5,2) on RTX 3070:

End-to-end: min=230µs, median=263µs, p90=308µs, max=2.5ms.

Plan shape: 1001 short rows, 0 medium, 0 long — **all work is in the short kernel**, like (4,4,2).

Row distribution (1001 rows, 8001 terms, mean 7.99):
- [1,1]:    25 rows  (2.5%)   [1 term]
- [2,4]:   240 rows  (24%)    [730 terms]
- [5,8]:   335 rows  (33.5%)  [2110 terms]   <- dominant bucket
- [9,16]:  320 rows  (32%)    [3590 terms]
- [17,31]:  81 rows  (8%)     [1546 terms]

Per-kernel (200 samples, CUDA.@elapsed mins):
- **short kernel (1 thread/row):    165 µs**
- **warp-per-row (long kernel WS=32): 43 µs**  <- **3.8x faster**

End-to-end 263 µs breakdown:
- short kernel:           165 µs  (63%)
- alloc/zero-init/sync:    98 µs  (37%)

Compared to (4,4,2): rows are larger (mean 8 vs 3.8) and more numerous (1001 vs 165), so kernel time grows but overhead stays ~constant. (5,5,2) is less overhead-dominated than (4,4,2).

GPUPolynomials.jl-d9b (warp-per-row default) is an even bigger win here than (4,4,2). Estimated end-to-end: 263 → 141 µs (~46% saved by warp-per-row alone).

== On the larger original array (126 monomials = 1008 B vs 35/280 B for (4,4,*)) ==

ideas.md idea #1 (shmem-cache of original) was no-op on (4,4,6) because 280 B fits in L2 trivially. Prediction for (5,5,2): still no-op. 1008 B = 8 cache lines, well within L1 capacity. Indirect-read pressure is ~30K reads/kernel (8001 terms x ~3-4 factors/term), all hitting an 8-line working set. The L1 cache absorbs this fully; explicitly stage-loading to shmem won't help.

The shmem cache idea would only become relevant when original is large enough to exceed L1 (tens of KB), which would correspond to inputs with thousands of monomials. None of the four benchmark cases approach that regime. Recommend NOT pursuing idea #1 unless future use cases bring much larger n_input.

title: Profile formula_pow for (n_vars=4, d=4, pow=2)
description: Profile the (4,4,2) benchmark case on RTX 3070 — ideas.md notes this is a 'short-rows-only path'. Confirm all work goes to the short kernel and identify the bottleneck there. Record per-kernel timing and candidate optimizations (e.g. warp-per-row for tiny rows, fused tiny-row kernel, short-row sort).
notes:
Profile (4,4,2) on RTX 3070:

End-to-end: min=134µs, median=161µs, p90=231µs, max=2.56ms (lighter tail than (4,8,3)).

Plan shape: 165 short rows, 0 medium, 0 long — **all work is in the short kernel**, as ideas.md predicted.

Row distribution (165 rows, 630 total terms, mean 3.82):
- [1,1]:   16 rows  (9.7%)
- [2,4]:   94 rows  (57%)   <- dominant bucket
- [5,8]:   54 rows  (33%)
- [9,16]:   1 row   (0.6%)

Per-kernel (200 samples, CUDA.@elapsed mins):
- **short kernel (1 thread/row):    69 µs**  <- current
- **warp-per-row via long kernel:   25 µs**  <- proposed (2.7x faster)

Breakdown of end-to-end 161 µs median:
- short kernel:           69 µs  (43%)
- alloc/zero-init/sync:   92 µs  (57%)

Confirms suggestion A from GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g: **warp-per-row for short tier is a big win here** (44 µs saved, ~27% end-to-end).

Note: 67% of short-tier rows have <=4 terms, so warp-per-row at 32 threads wastes ~28 threads per row. Still 2.7x faster than 1 thread/row, but this is exactly the scenario where the subwarp-per-row idea (GPUPolynomials.jl-jhq, B) could in principle help further. However, 25 µs is already small; diminishing returns likely make jhq not worthwhile.

The large overhead share (57% of end-to-end) makes this case ideal for GPUPolynomials.jl-63i (pre-alloc) + GPUPolynomials.jl-kwd (skip zero-init). If those together save 40 µs and warp-per-row saves 44 µs, end-to-end drops from 161 µs → ~77 µs (2x speedup on (4,4,2)).

title: Profile formula_pow for (n_vars=4, d=8, pow=3)
description: Profile the (4,8,3) benchmark case on RTX 3070. Identify which kernel is the bottleneck, the row-length distribution, and whether the WS_L=512 finding from (4,4,6) generalizes. Record per-kernel timing, row counts per tier, and candidate optimizations.
notes:
Profile (4,8,3) on RTX 3070:

End-to-end: min=212µs, median=251µs, p90=2885µs, max=13.2ms (heavy tail — 11x median at p90).

Per-kernel (CUDA.@elapsed mins, 200 samples):
- short kernel (WS=32):  47.6 µs  (35% of 135 µs kernel-sum)
- medium kernel (WS=32): 27.8 µs  (21%)
- long kernel (WS=256):  59.1 µs  (44%) ← largest but not dominant

Distribution (total 762K terms, 2925 rows):
- short tier: 566 rows, mean 14.9 terms, 1.1% of terms
- medium tier: 1338 rows, mean 112 terms, 19.6% of terms
- long tier: 1021 rows, max 1453, mean 592, 79% of terms
  - [256,511]: 534 rows (52% of long tier!)
  - [512,1023]: 376 rows
  - [1024,2047]: 111 rows
  - No rows >= 2048.

Key contrast vs (4,4,6): very different shape. (4,4,6) had max row 12,652; (4,8,3) maxes at 1453. Row distribution is medium-heavy, not long-heavy.

WS_L scan (long kernel only):
- WS=128:  61.2 µs
- WS=256:  59.1 µs  ← optimal
- WS=512:  68.3 µs  ← WORSE (wastes threads on the 534 [256,511] rows)
- WS=1024: 106.3 µs

IMPORTANT: WS_L=512 (the big win for (4,4,6)) is a LOSS here. The optimal WS depends on the row-length distribution — confirms GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g needs to be adaptive / tier-aware, not a fixed switch.

Observations:
- No single kernel dominates (44/35/21 split), so single-kernel optimizations have limited ceiling.
- Short kernel is the underutilized-occupancy suspect: 566 rows × 1 thread/row means ~36% of one SM's threads in flight. Upgrading short tier to warp-per-row (WS=32, 1 warp/row) could plausibly drop this to ~20 µs.
- Heavy tail latency (p90=11x median) warrants separate investigation — possibly alloc churn, GPU clock transitions, or kernel cache pressure.

Implication for fourth-tier feature (GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g): should be adaptive rather than fixed. A reasonable design might be: pick WS for rows ≥256 per-row based on row length, not globally. Alternatively: pick WS_L based on the HEAVIEST row lengths in the plan.

title: Redesign formula_pow tier partition (adaptive WS, extend warp-per-row to short tier)
description:
Tier partition in formula_pow needs to become adaptive and possibly extend in both directions. Profiling across (4,4,6), (4,8,3), and others (to come) shows the optimal WS per row depends strongly on the row-length distribution:

- (4,4,6): long tier goes up to 12,652 terms; WS_L=512 wins (25% faster than current 256).
- (4,8,3): long tier maxes at 1,453 terms with 52%% of rows in [256,511]; WS_L=512 is a LOSS vs 256.

So a single global WS_L threshold is wrong. Some combination of:

1. A new tier at WS=256 for rows 256..511 (original suggestion), keeping WS=512 only for rows >=512.
2. Adaptive tier boundary selection at plan time based on the row-length histogram (e.g. pick WS_L to match the median or p75 long-row length).
3. Moving the current tier thresholds (32/256) — are they still right once the long end is adjustable?

Also: extend warp-per-row down to the SHORT tier (suggestion A from the (4,8,3) profile discussion). Currently rows <32 terms use 1 thread/row. For (4,8,3) this gives 566 threads total, saturating only 0.8%% of the GPU; the short kernel is purely latency-bound. Warp-per-row (one warp per row at WS=32) was already applied to medium rows in commit 519fa7e — we can extend it to short rows by simply merging the short tier into the long-kernel path at WS=32.

Expected wins if done together:
- Warp-per-row for short: ~47µs -> ~20µs on (4,8,3) (~11%% end-to-end), ~121µs -> ~50µs on (4,4,6) (~7%%).
- Adaptive WS_L: ~25%% on (4,4,6), preserves (4,8,3).

Implementation constraints:
- formula_pow_plan currently caches the tier partition at first call keyed on (n_vars,d,pow) only (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl line 185). Silently ignores later workgroup_size kwargs. Either key on full config or separate the expensive Oscar expansion from the tier-partition step.
- All three tier kernels need to support their WS as a Val parameter (already the case for long kernel, not yet for short).

Planning is UNFINISHED — design the final partition scheme (fixed 4-tier? adaptive? data-driven?) before implementing. Validate on (4,4,6), (4,8,3), and the (4,4,2) / (5,5,2) profiles still to come.

title: Profile formula_pow to identify current bottleneck
description: Profile the current formula_pow benchmarks to identify the actual bottleneck, then evaluate whether the suggestions in ideas.md would help or whether a different optimization is warranted.
notes:
Profile of formula_pow @ (4,4,6) on RTX 3070, 50 warm calls via CUDA.@profile:

Per-call GPU time (total 881 µs):
- long kernel (WS=256):   714 µs (60%, processes 1641 rows w/ ≥256 terms = 97% of work)
- short kernel (WS=32):   121 µs (10%, 410 rows <32 terms)
- medium kernel (WS=32):   45 µs (3.7%, 874 rows 32-255 terms)

Row distribution: 2925 output rows, 3.838M total terms. Long-tier rows range 275..12652 terms, mean 2271.

Experiment: bumped long kernel WS from 256 → 512. Result: 492 µs vs 714 µs (**25% faster on long kernel, 29% end-to-end**: 1019→790 µs). Correctness verified. WS=64/128 are worse; WS=1024 slightly worse than 512.

Reassessment of ideas.md:
- #7 (WS tuning) was marked 'lower impact' but is actually the biggest lever.
- #2 (warp-shuffle reduction tail) is secondary; barrier cost at WS=512 is 9 barriers — saving 5 via shuffle could give ~5-10% more but requires native CUDA.
- #4 (sort short rows) only touches 10% of time.
- #6 (Int32 term_coeffs) ~4% estimated.
- #8 (fuse kernels) saves launch overhead ~30-50 µs (~5%).

New suggestion: now that WS_L=512 is optimal, add a fourth tier at WS=256 for rows 256-511 (~4% of work). Also, the plan cache currently bakes tier partition at first call regardless of workgroup_size kwarg — minor correctness issue.

title: Benchmark update: add mid-size config
description:
## Why
Current benchmark only exercises n_vars=4,d=4 (original=35 elements, 280B). Need a larger working set to prove the shmem-cache win generalizes and isn't a toy-size artifact. (6,4,4) gives original=84 elements (672B) — still cached, still under cap, but a 2.4x larger working set.

## What
- Add run_case(6, 4, 4) to benchmarks/formula_pow_vs_ntt_bench.jl.
- Record before/after numbers for (4,4,2), (4,4,6), (6,4,4) in this issue's notes via 'bd update <id> --append-notes'.

## Acceptance
- CUDA formula_pow median measurably lower on (4,4,6) and (6,4,4) vs pre-change.
- No regression on (4,4,2) (short-rows-only; cache overhead should be negligible at WS=256 / 35 elements).
close_reason: Superseded. Parent epic oek was abandoned — shmem-cache experiment on branch jjg/shmem-cache-experiment (commit d1481ac) showed no measurable improvement on RTX 3070 because the 280B original already fits in L2. The (6,4,4) mid-size benchmark was only there to prove cache generalization, which the experiment disproved.

title: Fallback path correctness test
description:
## Why
Existing Oscar-comparison tests in test/FormulaPowTests.jl run at (n_vars<=4, d<=4) where the cache path is always selected. Without an explicit fallback test, the uncached kernel path goes untested on CI — regressions there would only surface when someone runs a large config.

## What
- Add a test case to test/FormulaPowTests.jl at (4,4,2) that calls formula_pow(original, plan, backend; cache_cap_bytes = 0) to force CACHE=false.
- Compare output against the same Oscar f^pow reference used by existing tests.
- Keep pow=2 so the test stays fast.

## Acceptance
- Test passes locally and on CI.
- Test fails if the non-cached kernel code path is broken.
- Default cache_cap_bytes=16384 unchanged for all other callers.
close_reason: Added 'fallback path CUDA' testset in test/FormulaPowTests.jl. Calls formula_pow(...; cache_cap_bytes=0) at (4,4,2) to force CACHE=false and compares to Oscar f^pow. Test passes; no plan-cache pollution (knob is a call kwarg on formula_pow, not formula_pow_plan).

title: Long kernel: cached shared-memory path
description:
## Why
formula_pow_long_kernel! (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl:259) reads original[monomial_indices[kk]] inside phase-1's partial-sum loop, striped by workgroup_size. That's the hottest read-indirection in the pipeline; caching original collapses it to shmem reads.

## What
- Extend formula_pow_long_kernel! signature to (..., ::Val{WS}, ::Val{CACHE}, ::Val{CLEN}). Existing Val{WS} stays.
- CACHE=true body: a second @localmem eltype(output) (CLEN,) buffer alongside the existing WS-sized reduction shmem; add a phase 0 that cooperatively loads original via strided loop on lid; @synchronize before phase 1 runs.
- CACHE=false body: current kernel unchanged.
- formula_pow dispatches Val(cache) and Val(plan.cache_len) computed at call time (see epic).
- Preserve existing @synchronize-split convention: lid/row re-derived from gidx in each phase (see lines 269-272 for the pattern).

## Acceptance
- Existing tests at (4,4) pass.
- Output matches CACHE=false variant bit-for-bit.
close_reason: Long kernel: added Val{CACHE}, Val{CLEN} type params alongside existing Val{WS}. Second @localmem (shmem_orig) for the original cache coexists with existing reduction shmem. Phase 0: cooperative strided load via @index(Local,Linear) + @synchronize, gated by if CACHE (specializes away when false). Preserved existing @synchronize-split convention — gidx assigned via @index(Global,Linear) between Phase 0 and Phase 1 so it's available in both. All subsequent phases unchanged. CUDA tests pass.

title: Short kernel: cached shared-memory path
description:
## Why
formula_pow_short_kernel! (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl:222) reads original[monomial_indices[k]] on every iteration of the inner term loop. At (4,4,6) that's hundreds of thousands of uncoalesced global reads for just the short-row portion. Caching original once per workgroup collapses those to shmem reads.

## What
- Extend formula_pow_short_kernel! signature with two type params: ::Val{CACHE} and ::Val{CLEN}.
- CACHE=true body: shmem = @localmem eltype(output) (CLEN,); cooperative strided load of original keyed on @index(Local); @synchronize; inner loop reads shmem[monomial_indices[k]] instead of original[...].
- CACHE=false body: current kernel unchanged (kept as the fallback).
- Update formula_pow (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl:324): compute cache = plan.cache_len * sizeof(eltype(original)) <= cache_cap_bytes; pass Val(cache) and Val(plan.cache_len) to the kernel.
- Launch with explicit groupsize=WS (current short kernel has no explicit workgroup_size — required for cooperative shmem load).

## Acceptance
- Existing tests at (4,4) pass (cache path).
- Output byte-identical to pre-change at the same seed.
close_reason: Short kernel: added Val{WS}, Val{CACHE}, Val{CLEN} type params. Single kernel (not two) — the CACHE=true/false specialization at JIT handles conditional @synchronize safely since the if CACHE branch is eliminated at compile time. @localmem always declared; formula_pow passes Val(1) for CLEN when cache=false so fallback allocation is 1 element. ndrange padded to WS multiple for correctness of the cooperative cache load; bounds-guarded main loop. CUDA tests at (3,2,2) and (4,4,6) Int128 pass.

title: Plan: add cache_len field to FormulaPowPlan
description:
## Why
Kernels need the length of original at JIT-compile time to allocate @localmem with a static size. Storing it on the plan once (computed from (n_vars, d) at plan build) avoids recomputing and lets formula_pow dispatch Val{CLEN}-parameterized kernels.

The cache-vs-fallback decision itself does NOT live on the plan under design (B) — it's computed at call time in formula_pow from plan.cache_len * sizeof(eltype(original)) <= cache_cap_bytes.

## What
- Add cache_len::Int field to FormulaPowPlan (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl:60).
- In formula_pow_plan (src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl:176): compute cache_len = binomial(n_vars + d - 1, d) and pass to the constructor.
- No changes to _formula_pow_cache (keyed on (n_vars, d, pow)).

## Non-goals
- Do NOT add cache_original::Bool to the plan — that decision is at call time.
- Do NOT add cache_cap_bytes to formula_pow_plan — it's a kwarg on formula_pow.
- Do NOT change the plan cache key or value shape.

## Acceptance
- FormulaPowPlan struct has cache_len field populated correctly for varied (n_vars, d).
- Existing tests pass with the added field (no behavior change yet — kernels don't use cache_len until .2/.3 land).
close_reason: Added cache_len::Int field to FormulaPowPlan; formula_pow_plan computes cache_len = binomial(n_vars+d-1, d). No cache_original Bool and no cache_cap_bytes on plan (per design B). Existing tests green.

title: Cache original in shared memory for CUDA formula_pow
description:
## Why
CUDA formula_pow runs at ~2.2ms vs NTT at ~1.4ms for (n_vars=4,d=4,pow=6) on RTX 3070. Kernel analysis (ideas.md) shows both short-row and long-row kernels indirect-index original[monomial_indices[k]] millions of times per invocation, producing uncoalesced global-memory reads. original is only 35 Int64s (280B) in that config — trivially fits in shared memory.

## What
Cache original in on-chip shared memory (@localmem) at the start of each workgroup in both kernels. Stays within KernelAbstractions — no native CUDA kernel needed (reserved for sibling ideas #2/#3 in ideas.md).

## Design (choice B — call-time dispatch)
- cache_len::Int is the only new field on FormulaPowPlan (length of original, determined by (n_vars, d) at plan build).
- cache_cap_bytes::Int = 16_384 is a kwarg on formula_pow itself — NOT on formula_pow_plan. Default 16KB leaves ~32KB shmem/block headroom under CUDA's 48KB default, after the existing 2KB reduction buffer at WS=256.
- formula_pow computes cache = plan.cache_len * sizeof(eltype(original)) <= cache_cap_bytes at call time and dispatches Val{CACHE}-parameterized kernels.
- Kernels take Val{CACHE} + Val{CLEN} type params; CACHE picks cached vs direct-read body at JIT time (no runtime branch in the hot loop); CLEN gives @localmem a static size.
- The module-level _formula_pow_cache (keyed on (n_vars,d,pow)) stays element-type-agnostic — one cached plan serves Int64, Int128, and Int32 original arrays without staleness.
- WS=256 for short kernel to match long kernel (required for cooperative shmem load).

## Rationale for (B) over (A)
- Plan cache key stays (n_vars,d,pow); baking eltype_hint into a cache_original Bool would either lie for callers of a different eltype or force a broader cache key.
- Kernels are already polymorphic over Int32/Int64/Int128 originals; pinning the plan to one eltype discards that.
- Test knob (cache_cap_bytes=0 to force fallback) is a call-time kwarg — no plan-cache pollution.
- Runtime cost at call site: one multiply + one compare, negligible next to ~10us CUDA launch.

## Files
- src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl
- test/FormulaPowTests.jl
- benchmarks/formula_pow_vs_ntt_bench.jl

## Acceptance
- Existing Oscar-comparison tests pass (cache path).
- New fallback test passes (forces uncached path via cache_cap_bytes=0).
- Benchmark shows measurable improvement on (4,4,6) and (6,4,4); no regression on (4,4,2).

title: On-disk plan cache for formula_pow_plan
description:
formula_pow_plan currently caches CSR data in a module-level Dict (_formula_pow_cache, src/algorithms/gpu/formula_pow.jl line 8) keyed on (n_vars, d, pow). Cache is lost on Julia restart, package reload, or any out-of-process invocation.

== Why ==

Plan construction at high pow is dominated by Oscar's sum(avars)^pow expansion and expressions_from_poly's term iteration. Measured first-build times on this workstation (2026-04-24):

  (4,4,6): 288 s (4.8 min)
  (4,8,3): 202 s
  (5,5,2):   1.0 s
  (4,4,2):   0.02 s

For the high-pow cases, every fresh Julia session costs minutes. During development of the tier/batching design, this is painful enough that disk persistence is worth the implementation cost.

== What to cache ==

Cache only the EXPENSIVE bit: the five raw CSR arrays (term_ptr, term_coeffs, monomial_ptr, monomial_indices, monomial_degrees). Do NOT cache the tier partition (short_rows / medium_rows / long_rows) — that is computed cheaply from term_ptr at plan-construct time, and changing tier strategy (e.g. GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g) should not invalidate the disk cache.

== Format ==

Plain Julia Serialization stdlib is sufficient — five Int vectors serialize fast and compress well. Approximate sizes:

  (4,4,6): ~150-200 MB
  (4,8,3): ~30-50 MB
  (5,5,2):  <2 MB
  (4,4,2):  <100 KB

Mandatory: a format version stamp embedded in the file. A change to expressions_from_poly's CSR encoding (or a switch to padded layout — see deferral note below) MUST invalidate cached files cleanly. Mismatched version => recompute.

Filename: plan_<n_vars>_<d>_<pow>_v<FORMAT_VERSION>.jls.

Cache location: prefer user-cache dir (e.g. ~/.cache/GPUPolynomials/plans/ on Linux, equivalent via Scratch.jl or DataDeps.jl). Pkg-relative cache pollutes the install dir.

== Deferred until layout decision ==

DO NOT IMPLEMENT YET. Whether to adopt a padded-CSR layout (ideas.md #9) is an open architectural decision that will land via the tier redesign / batching work. Padded CSR changes the on-disk format completely. Implementing this bead before that decision means either:
  (a) shipping a format that gets invalidated almost immediately, or
  (b) building disk persistence twice.

Wait for the layout to settle (via GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g, GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj, and the per-row factor-count uniformity analysis already done in this session). Then implement against the chosen layout.

== Implementation sketch (when unblocked) ==

  - serialize_plan_csr(path, csr) writes version + 5 arrays
  - deserialize_plan_csr(path) reads + version-checks
  - formula_pow_plan checks disk before falling through to expressions_from_poly
  - In-session Dict cache stays as a hot path on top
  - ~50-100 lines

Optional follow-up: ship precomputed plans for common (n_vars, d, pow) tuples in the package itself (or as an artifact). Trades off package size vs first-use latency. Decide separately.

title: Add (5,5,2) and (4,8,3) to formula_pow_bench.jl (CPU vs Metal)
description:
benchmarks/formula_pow_bench.jl (the CPU vs Metal benchmark) currently only runs (4,4,2) and (4,4,6). The CUDA benchmark (formula_pow_vs_ntt_bench.jl) covers all four cases — (4,4,2), (4,4,6), (5,5,2), (4,8,3) — but the CPU/Metal version is missing (5,5,2) and (4,8,3).

Add the two missing cases so cross-backend regressions get caught for all four tracked benchmark tuples. Same call shape as existing cases:

    run_case(5, 5, 2, Int64)
    run_case(4, 8, 3, Int64)

Trivial change. Useful before tier/batching work lands so we can compare KA-on-CPU and Metal numbers against the CUDA profiles.

title: Investigate subwarp-per-row kernel for very short rows
description:
The short tier (<32 terms) includes rows as small as 1-4 terms. If we extend warp-per-row (32 threads/row) to these rows via GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g, we'll waste many threads per warp on 1-term rows (31 idle) and 4-term rows (28 idle).

A subwarp-per-row kernel could pack multiple tiny rows into one warp — e.g. 8 rows per warp with 4 threads/row, reducing across a sub-group rather than a full warp.

Open questions to investigate:
- What fraction of short-tier rows are truly tiny (<=4 terms) vs nearly-full (20-31 terms) across (4,4,2), (4,4,6), (4,8,3), (5,5,2)?
- Is the waste meaningful vs the simpler warp-per-row from GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g? If 95%% of short-tier rows are >=16 terms, subwarp-per-row is probably not worth the complexity.
- Can this be expressed in KernelAbstractions or does it require native CUDA / CUDA.shfl_sync primitives?

Decision gate: only pursue this if GPUPolynomials.jl-d3g is landed AND the remaining short-kernel cost is a meaningful fraction of end-to-end time AND row-length histograms show a tiny-row-heavy tail.

Likely to be dropped — file for completeness.
close_reason: Closed pre-implementation. Empirical analysis (warp-divergence sweep, 2026-04-25) showed sort + K1 (1 thread/row) achieves >99% warp efficiency across all four benchmark cases at B>=100, perfectly saturated at B>=1000. Subwarp packings (8x4 / 16x2 / 4x8) would only help in an intermediate B=10-100 regime that we don't target — workload is either single-op (B=1, where K2 wins) or large-scale batched (B>=1000, where K1 wins). No use case justifies the maintenance cost of a packing kernel. See notes on GPUPolynomials.jl-6jj for the locked design.
